GREEK THEATRE
Lesson 2 · Sources and Notes

What did the theatre look like, and how did it work?

OCR A Level Classical Civilisation · H408/21 Greek Theatre · w/c 2 Nov 2026

Step 1 · 4 images

Walking into the theatre: theatron, orchestra, eisodoi

The story of this step · read this first

The plays you are studying were first performed in the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, on the south slope of the Acropolis. Below it was the sanctuary of Dionysus, the god of the festival.

The theatre you see in photographs is not the one Sophocles knew. In the fifth century the seats were wooden benches and the building at the back was wood too. In the 330s BC the theatre was rebuilt in stone, and the Romans changed it again later.

A Greek theatre had three main parts. The theatron, “the watching place”, was the seating on the hillside, where thousands of people sat looking down. The orchestra, “the dancing place”, was the flat floor at the bottom, where the chorus sang and danced and the actors performed. The eisodoi, “the ways in”, were the two side paths by which everyone came on and went off. The paths were long, so characters in the plays often announce who is coming.

The theatre at Epidaurus (Image 4) is the best-preserved Greek theatre, so it shows all three parts clearly. But it was built about 340 BC, later than our plays, and it is not in Athens.

No written sources in this step. The images above are the evidence.

Where this leaves us

The theatron was the seating on the hillside, the orchestra was the dancing floor, and the eisodoi were the two side paths. In the fifth century it was all wood; the stone theatre in Athens today was built in the 330s BC.

Step 2 · 1 image

Thorikos: a village theatre

The story of this step · read this first

Attica was divided into villages and districts called demes, and many of them had their own small theatre for their own festival of Dionysus. Thorikos, on the south-east coast near the silver mines, is the best preserved. It was in use by about 500 BC. It is a prescribed source, so you must be able to describe it.

The seats are in a long bank that is nearly straight and curves only at the ends. It held about 3,000 people. The floor is shaped like a rectangle with rounded corners. There was a small temple of Dionysus at one end of the floor and an altar at the side. There is no sign of a building at the back.

Epidaurus has a round floor, and Thorikos does not. Textbook drawings of Athens show a round floor, but because of Thorikos many scholars think the early floor at Athens may not have been round either. Nobody knows for certain.

No written sources in this step. The images above are the evidence.

Where this leaves us

Thorikos is a village theatre in Attica, in use by about 500 BC: a long, nearly straight bank of seats, a floor shaped like a rounded rectangle, a temple and altar of Dionysus, and no building at the back. Early theatres were not always round.

Step 3 · 3 sources · 1 image

The skene: the door and the roof

The story of this step · read this first

Skene means “tent” or “hut”. At first it was probably a hut where the actors changed their masks. By about 460 BC it had become part of the play: a wooden building at the back of the orchestra, with a large door in the middle and a flat roof. Our words “scene” and “scenery” come from skene.

The roof. In Aeschylus’ Agamemnon (458 BC), the first play we have that needs a building, the first character is a watchman lying on the palace roof (S1). Queen Clytemnestra has posted him there to watch for the beacon fires that will tell her Troy has fallen.

The door was the most important place in the theatre. The audience could see the outside of the house but not the inside. In Agamemnon the king walks through the door, and his wife Clytemnestra kills him inside, in his bath; the audience only hears his screams. In the next play their son Orestes comes home to avenge his father, and has to get in through the same door (S2). In Greek tragedy violent deaths almost always happen inside. In Oedipus the King, Jocasta goes in and hangs herself, and Oedipus goes in and blinds himself.

The front of the skene was painted, but there was no built set for each play, because three or four plays were performed in one day. The characters told the audience what the building was. At the start of Bacchae (S3), Dionysus tells the audience that they are in Thebes, that the building is the palace of Cadmus, and that next to it is the smoking tomb of his mother Semele. Semele was a Theban princess loved by Zeus. Jealous Hera tricked her into asking Zeus to show himself in his true form; he appeared as lightning and she was burned to death. Zeus saved her unborn child, Dionysus.

S1Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1–7 (458 BC)The watchman on the roof

Context The first lines of the Oresteia. A watchman lies on the palace roof, waiting for the beacon fire that will tell Clytemnestra that Troy has fallen.

WATCHMAN: I ask the gods for release from these labours, this watch a year long, in which, couched on my elbows on the roof of the house of Atreus like a dog, I have come to know the gathering of the night stars, and those bright lords that bring winter and summer to mortals, the shining powers conspicuous in the sky, when they set and when they rise.

What it shows
  • The first surviving play that needs a building (458 BC).
  • The skene had a roof strong enough for an actor.
S2Aeschylus, Libation Bearers 653–67 (458 BC)Orestes knocks at the palace door

Context The second play of the Oresteia. Orestes has come home in disguise to kill his mother, Clytemnestra. He has to get into the palace.

ORESTES: Boy! Boy! Hear my knocking at the courtyard door. Who is inside? Boy, boy, again, who is at home? A third time I call for someone to come out of the house, if Aegisthus has made it a house that welcomes strangers. SERVANT: All right, I hear you. Where is the stranger from, and where? ORESTES: Announce me to the masters of the house, to whom I have come bringing news. And be quick, for the dark chariot of night is hurrying on, and it is time for travellers to drop anchor in a house that receives all comers. Let someone with authority come out, the woman who is in charge, or, more fittingly, the man.

What it shows
  • A door you can knock on, with a servant behind it.
  • The audience sees the outside of the house but not the inside.
S3Euripides, Bacchae 1–12 (405 BC)Dionysus tells the audience where they are

Context The opening of the set tragedy. The god Dionysus, disguised as a man, speaks alone.

DIONYSUS: I have come, the son of Zeus, to this Theban land, Dionysus, whom Cadmus’ daughter Semele once bore, delivered by the lightning’s fire. Changing my shape from god to mortal I am here at the streams of Dirce and the water of Ismenus. I see the tomb of my mother, the thunder-struck one, here by the house, and the ruins of her home smouldering with the still-living flame of Zeus’ fire, Hera’s undying outrage against my mother. I praise Cadmus, who made this ground untrodden, a precinct for his daughter; I have covered it round with the clustering green of the vine.

What it shows
  • The words tell the audience where they are: Thebes, the palace of Cadmus, the tomb of Semele.
  • No built set was needed.
Where this leaves us

The skene was a wooden building at the back of the orchestra, from about 460 BC, with a door and a flat roof. The roof is first used in Agamemnon (458 BC). The door divided what the audience could see from what it could not, and deaths happened inside. The words of the play told the audience what the building was.

Step 4 · 2 sources

The ekkyklema: showing what happened inside

The story of this step · read this first

Deaths happen inside, but the playwright often wants the audience to see the bodies. The answer was the ekkyklema, “the thing rolled out”: a low wooden platform on wheels, pushed out through the skene door with the bodies arranged on it. The audience understood that they were now looking at the inside of the house.

You can spot it in a play when someone calls for the doors to be opened. In Hippolytus, Queen Phaedra has fallen in love with her stepson Hippolytus. He rejects her, and in shame she hangs herself, leaving a letter that falsely accuses him of rape. Her husband Theseus comes home and orders the doors opened (S4), and her body is rolled out.

Comedy made jokes about it. In Aristophanes’ Acharnians (S5), the playwright Euripides is too busy to come down, so he is “wheeled out” on the machine his own tragedies used for dead bodies.

S4Euripides, Hippolytus 808–10 (428 BC)Theseus orders the doors opened

Context Queen Phaedra has hanged herself inside the palace. Her husband Theseus has just come home.

THESEUS: Loose the bolts of the doors, servants, undo the fastenings, so that I may see the bitter sight of my wife, who by her death has destroyed me.

What it shows
  • The signal for the ekkyklema: a call to open the doors.
  • Phaedra’s body is then rolled out.
S5Aristophanes, Acharnians 403–11 (425 BC)Euripides is wheeled out

Context A comedy. Dicaeopolis has come to the house of the playwright Euripides to borrow a costume. Euripides is too busy writing to come down.

DICAEOPOLIS: Euripides! Dear little Euripides! Listen, if you ever listened to any man. It is Dicaeopolis of Cholleidae calling you, me. EURIPIDES: I have no time. DICAEOPOLIS: Then have yourself wheeled out. EURIPIDES: Impossible. DICAEOPOLIS: All the same. EURIPIDES: Very well, I will be wheeled out; I have no time to come down. DICAEOPOLIS: Euripides! EURIPIDES: Why are you shouting? DICAEOPOLIS: You compose with your feet up when you could do it on the ground? No wonder you make cripples.

What it shows
  • Comedy jokes about the ekkyklema: Euripides is wheeled out on it.
  • The audience knew the machine well.
Where this leaves us

The ekkyklema was a wheeled platform rolled out through the skene door to show what had happened inside, usually the dead. In Hippolytus Theseus calls for the doors to be opened first. In Acharnians Aristophanes has Euripides wheeled out on it.

Step 5 · 2 sources

The mechane: flying

The story of this step · read this first

The mechane, “the machine”, was a crane behind the skene. It had a long arm, a rope and a harness, and could lift an actor above the roof and swing them out over the stage.

Its first certain use in tragedy is Euripides’ Medea (431 BC). Medea, a princess from Colchis and granddaughter of the Sun, had helped Jason win the Golden Fleece. In Corinth Jason left her to marry the king’s daughter. Medea killed the bride with a poisoned dress and crown, and then killed her own two sons so that Jason would have no children. As Jason hammers on the doors, Medea appears above the house in a chariot drawn by dragons, with the children’s bodies (S6). She is out of his reach.

The crane was mostly used for gods appearing at the end of a play to sort out the plot. This gives us the Latin phrase deus ex machina, “the god from the machine”, which now means any sudden, convenient rescue at the end of a story. Comedy made fun of it: in Aristophanes’ Peace, the farmer Trygaeus flies to the gods on a giant dung-beetle and panics, shouting at the man working the crane (S7).

S6Euripides, Medea 1317–22 (431 BC)Medea above the house in the chariot of the Sun

Context Medea has killed her two sons. Jason is hammering on the doors to reach them. Medea appears above the house in a flying chariot with the bodies.

MEDEA: Why do you shake these doors and try to unbar them, seeking the corpses and me who did the deed? Stop this labour. If you need anything from me, say what you wish; but you shall never touch me with your hand. Such a chariot the Sun, my father’s father, gives me, a defence against the hand of enemies.

What it shows
  • The first certain use of the mechane (431 BC).
  • Medea above, out of reach; Jason below at the door.
S7Aristophanes, Peace 173–6 (421 BC)Trygaeus talks to the crane operator

Context A comedy. The farmer Trygaeus is flying up to the gods on a giant dung-beetle to bring back the goddess Peace.

TRYGAEUS: Oh, how frightened I am, and I am not joking now. You there, machine-operator, pay attention to me! There is already a wind churning round my navel, and if you are not careful I shall end up feeding the beetle.

What it shows
  • Proves the crane existed and needed an operator.
  • Comedy makes fun of the machine.
Where this leaves us

The mechane was a crane that lifted actors into the air. Its first certain use is Medea (431 BC). It was mostly used for gods at the end of a play, which gives us deus ex machina. Comedy made fun of it in Peace.

Step 6 · 1 source · 2 images

The theatre on pots

The story of this step · read this first

There are no photographs of Greek plays. The nearest thing is paintings on pottery. Three vases are prescribed. For each one you need to describe it and say how far it matches the plays. A painting is not a photograph: the painter may change things, or may be painting the story and not the performance.

The Perseus Dance Vase (textbook Fig. 1.10, p. 17) was made in Athens about 420 BC. A comic actor dressed as the hero Perseus, who cut off the head of the Gorgon Medusa, dances on a low platform holding a sickle and the bag with the head. Two men sit and watch. It is the only Athenian painting of a stage and the only ancient picture of a theatre audience.

The Medea krater (Image 7) was painted in southern Italy about 400 BC. A krater is a large bowl for mixing wine with water. Medea is above in a chariot pulled by snakes, inside a circle of sun-rays; her dead sons lie below with the nurse and the tutor; Jason looks up at her. It matches the play because Medea is above and Jason below. It does not match because in Euripides she takes the bodies with her, and there are no Furies in the play.

The Würzburg Telephus vase (Image 8) was painted in southern Italy about 370 BC. It shows Aristophanes’ comedy Women at the Thesmophoria. A relative of Euripides sneaks into a women-only festival dressed as a woman. When he is caught, he grabs a “baby” and threatens to kill it on the altar, but the baby turns out to be a wineskin wearing slippers (S8). The vase matches the play closely, and shows that Athenian plays were known in other parts of the Greek world forty years later.

Also used in this stepS6 Euripides, Medea 1317–22 (431 BC) (Step 5)
S8Aristophanes, Women at the Thesmophoria 689–95, 733–8 and 754–5 (411 BC)The wineskin baby

Context A comedy. A man disguised as a woman has been caught spying on a women’s festival. He grabs a woman’s “baby” and threatens to kill it on the altar.

(689–95) KINSMAN: Scream away; you will never feed this child again unless you let me go. Here, on the altar, struck by this knife, it will stain the altar with its bloody veins. WOMAN: No, I beg you! Have pity on me, not on the child … (733–8) KINSMAN: Who is this? Why, it is a wineskin full of wine, and wearing Persian slippers. O women, so hot for drink, so ingenious at finding ways to a cup, a great blessing to tavern-keepers and a curse to us, and to our crockery and our weaving. (754–5) WOMAN: Spare it, spare it! Or if you are going to cut its throat, at least give me a bowl to catch the blood.

What it shows
  • The scene painted on the Würzburg Telephus vase.
  • The “baby” is a wineskin in slippers.
Where this leaves us

The Perseus Dance Vase shows a comic actor on a low platform with two spectators. The Medea krater shows Medea above Jason, as in the play, but changes the ending. The Würzburg Telephus matches its comedy closely. Vases are useful evidence, but they must be checked against the plays.
